samples.summary: `remove()` writes a full document archive to disk without consulting `isPersistenceEnabled` / `isOfflineWritePermitted`, so content can be re-materialized after the user revoked consent
samples.evidence:
`refuseIfDisabled()` is called on exactly three write paths — `saveSnapshot` (line 619), `appendChange` (661) and `saveMeta` (708). `remove()` (795-854) is a fourth write path: at line 840 it `put`s an `ArchiveRecord` carrying `record.snapshot`, `header?.meta` and the whole compressed change log into the `archives` object store, and it consults neither `this.isPersistenceEnabled` nor the erase denial.

Vector: the user switches the Settings toggle off. `watchForOfflineDisable` (offline-erase.ts:581) fires with `getOfflinePersistenceEnabled()` already false and starts `eraseOfflineData` → `dropAllForUser`, which purges headers/snapshots and only then calls `dropArchivesWhere(BY_USER, …)`. By design the durable client is deliberately left mounted across the toggle (collab-document-provider.tsx:232-255). If the SDK emits `LocalChangesDropped` and calls `remove(docKey)` during that window — or after the archive-drop half has already run — line 840 writes the full document snapshot back into `archives`. Nothing re-runs the erase, so that content sits on the disk the user just asked to be cleared until the thirty-day sweep. The same window exists on the logout path: `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout` calls `denyOfflineWrites(who)` first (offline-erase.ts:330) specifically so live writes are refused for the duration of the erase, and `remove()` is the one write that ignores that denial.

The other three writers were given the guard for exactly this reason; `remove()` was missed. A `refuseIfDisabled(docKey)` (or an `isOfflineWritePermitted` check) before the `put` at 840 closes it — deleting without archiving is the correct behaviour once the user has asked for the content to be gone.

samples.summary: The offline opt-in is keyed per *device* only, so one account's consent causes a different account's document content to be written to that machine's disk without that user ever being asked
samples.evidence:
`STORAGE_KEY = "wafflebase-offline-persistence"` is a single, unqualified `localStorage` key — there is no user component. `CollabDocumentProvider` reads it through `useOfflinePersistenceEnabled()` and combines it only with `supportsClientKey()`, `permitted` and the signed-in identity (collab-document-provider.tsx:217-229); nothing checks *who* turned it on.

Vector, on the shared machine this feature's threat model is built around: user A signs in, enables "Save documents on this device", and signs out (or their session simply expires). The preference survives — it is device-local by design. User B then signs in on the same browser profile; `useOfflinePersistenceEnabled()` returns true for them, `useDurableDocument` elects their tab, and every document B opens is written to that disk under B's own store scope. B was never shown the toggle, never agreed to it, and the Settings switch will read as already-on if they ever look.

The design doc reasons carefully about the opposite direction only — `docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md` § Turning it on argues an account-level setting "would follow the user onto a shared machine and re-enable there" — and does not address that a device-level setting applies to every subsequent user of that device. B's exposure is bounded by B's own deliberate sign-out, but the consent that caused it was A's. Scoping the preference key by user id (`wafflebase-offline-persistence:{userId}`) preserves the per-device property the design wants while making the consent the actual user's.

samples.summary: An expired session (401) erases nothing, leaving the signed-out user's full document content plus their client-key salts readable on a shared device for up to thirty days
samples.evidence:
`fetchWithAuth`'s 401 arm passes `eraseLocalData: "none"`, and `logout()` gates the erase on `eraseLocalData !== "none" && res?.ok`, so `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout()` never runs. It also never records a pending erase, so `retryPendingOfflineErase()` (offline-erase.ts:360) has nothing to finish.

Consequence on the shared workstation the design names as the motivating case: user A's IndexedDB snapshots, change logs and archives — full document text — remain on the origin after their session ends involuntarily, which is the *common* way a session ends. The next person at that profile can read every one of them directly via devtools; IndexedDB is origin-scoped, not session-scoped. Their `wafflebase-durable-device:{userId}:{docKey}` salts survive alongside (durable-session.ts:142), so the next user can also reconstruct A's per-document Yorkie client keys — the exact derivation the salt exists to prevent (durable-session.ts:80-104) — though by then they already hold the plaintext.

The only bounds are `collectStale`'s thirty-day age and `sweepStaleSecrets`'s matching thirty days. The tradeoff is deliberate and documented (erasing would destroy the un-pushed change log on an event the user did not choose), so this is flagged as an accepted-risk note rather than a defect in the branch taken — but thirty days of retained document content after the authority to read it ended is worth an explicit decision rather than a side effect of the 401 arm. A middle path exists: drop the *live snapshot* on 401 while keeping the change log and archives, which preserves the unsent work without leaving the full document body behind.

samples.summary: `randomSecret()` falls back to `Math.random()` for the client-key salt, whose entire purpose is to be unguessable
samples.evidence:
Lines 244-257: when `crypto.getRandomValues` is unavailable the salt is built from `Math.floor(Math.random() * 256)`. `Math.random()` is not a CSPRNG — V8 seeds xorshift128+ per context and its output is recoverable from a short observed sequence — so a salt minted on this path is predictable rather than merely weak.

That salt is the only thing standing between a workspace peer and another member's Yorkie client key: `durableClientKey` is `wb:{deviceSecret}:{userId}:{docKey}`, and the file's own comment (lines 80-104) states that Yorkie authorizes `ActivateClient`/`DeactivateClient` on token validity alone, so a derivable key lets any member with a valid token tear down another member's per-document client and strand their durable session. The other two ingredients are public to a peer.

The inline comment argues the branch is unreachable because `navigator.locks` and `crypto` are both secure-context APIs, which is a reasonable claim — hence low impact — but the fallback is reachable in any environment where `crypto` is shimmed away or a non-secure-context caller reaches `durableClientKey` directly (it is an exported function with no gate of its own). Throwing, or refusing durability, is the safer failure than minting a predictable salt: the surrounding module already fails closed everywhere else (`supportsDurableSession`, the `.catch(() => undefined)` at line 432).

samples.summary: An archive of a headerless entry is attributed to whoever is signed in now (`?? this.userId`), which would make another account's document content listable and recoverable by the current user
samples.evidence:
Line 838: `userId: header?.userId ?? this.userId`. Every read-side access control on archives keys on that field — `listArchives()` uses `index(BY_USER).getAll(this.userId)` (1066) and `loadArchive()` refuses `row.userId !== this.userId` (1090). So the fallback is the one place where an archive's owner is *asserted* rather than carried.

If a snapshot row ever exists without its header row, `remove()` reaches line 829 with `record` truthy and `header` undefined, and stamps the archive with the currently signed-in user. That archive then appears in their `listArchives()`, `rehydrateArchive` decompresses it, and `recoverOfflineCopy` materializes it as a real document in *their* workspace (`offline-copy-recovery.ts:301`) — a full cross-account content disclosure plus a persistent copy with the wrong name on it.

I could not complete the chain to a reachable producer of a headerless snapshot, which is why confidence is low: `atomically` (1385-1401) now aborts a torn `saveSnapshot`, `orphanSnapshotKeys()` collects such rows in `collectStale`, and `remove()` is only ever called by the SDK for a key whose `clientKey` segment embeds the current user. But the failure mode is severe and the safe form costs nothing: skip the archive (or refuse it) when `header` is absent, rather than claiming ownership of bytes whose owner is unknown. The neighbouring comment at 843-846 explicitly acknowledges "a header without one is a shape a torn write can produce", so the code already assumes the state is reachable.

verdict.reason: Verified in-repo. `refuseIfDisabled()` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:404-413) is invoked on only three write paths — saveSnapshot:619, appendChange:661, saveMeta:708. `remove()` (795-854) is a fourth writer: lines 829-841 assemble an ArchiveRecord containing `record.snapshot`, `header?.meta` and the entire compressed change log and `put` it into the ARCHIVES store at line 840, with no consultation of `this.isPersistenceEnabled` and no consultation of the erase denial (`isOfflineWritePermitted`, offline-erase.ts:208-213). The denial is real and is deliberately raised before any row is deleted on logout (denyOfflineWrites at offline-erase.ts:330) exactly so a still-mounted durable client cannot write during the erase; the preference+denial pair is wired into the store only via `isPersistenceEnabled` (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:185-186), which `remove()` ignores. Reachability holds: the store is passed unwrapped to the SDK (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:234, KeyedYorkieProvider cast at 49-51), `DurableLossWatch` latches `expectLoss` on `local-changes-dropped` (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:310), and the client is intentionally left mounted across the toggle (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:172-186) while `watchForOfflineDisable` runs `eraseOfflineData` un-awaited (offline-erase.ts:581-609). `dropAllForUser` purges headers/snapshots first and only then drops archives (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1121-1165), so an interleaved or post-erase `remove()` can land a full snapshot in `archives` — and residual windows survive the common ordering (a purge that throws aborts before dropArchivesWhere at line 1162; orphan snapshot rows are never enumerated by the header-index walk at line 1125). No guard, wrapper, or caller-side check makes line 840 unreachable when persistence is revoked, so none of not-present / already-guarded / out-of-scope applies; retaining full document content on disk after an explicit erase or sign-out is sensitive-data exposure in this lens's lane.

verdict.reason: The code is exactly as described. `STORAGE_KEY = "wafflebase-offline-persistence"` (offline-persistence-preference.ts:19) is a single device-global localStorage key with no user component; `getOfflinePersistenceEnabled` (line 48) reads it unqualified. `collab-document-provider.tsx:217-223` combines it only with `supportsClientKey()` and `permitted`, and `use-durable-document.ts:127-132` gates on `supportsClientKey() && permitted && enabled && !!userId` — `userId` only scopes the store/client key, it never qualifies whose consent `enabled` represents. I enumerated all callers of the preference (settings/page.tsx:128, sync-status-chip.tsx:102, durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:186, offline-erase.ts:579, PrivateRoute.tsx:25) and none clears or re-scopes it on sign-out, so A's opt-in survives into B's session. The only per-user gate, `isOfflineWritePermitted` (offline-erase.ts:208-213), is an erase-deny list that returns true for an account with no prior erase and is re-permitted on sign-in (offline-erase.ts:192-195) — it is not a consent gate, so it does not make this unreachable. The design doc addresses only the inverse case (offline-persistence-preference.ts:7-12; docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md:220-241), and per doc lines 206-218 the 401/expiry path erases nothing, so B's document content can persist on that disk without B ever consenting. This is sensitive-data-at-rest exposure without the data subject's consent on the shared-device threat model the feature is built for — in the Security lane and blocking at major.

finding.evidence:
Line 838: `userId: header?.userId ?? this.userId`. Every read-side access control on archives keys on that field — `listArchives()` uses `index(BY_USER).getAll(this.userId)` (1066) and `loadArchive()` refuses `row.userId !== this.userId` (1090). If a snapshot row ever exists without its header row, `remove()` reaches line 829 with `record` truthy and `header` undefined, and stamps the archive with the currently signed-in user. That archive then appears in their `listArchives()`, `rehydrateArchive` decompresses it, and `recoverOfflineCopy` materializes it as a real document in *their* workspace (`offline-copy-recovery.ts:301`) — a full cross-account content disclosure plus a persistent copy with the wrong name on it.

I could not complete the chain to a reachable producer of a headerless snapshot, which is why confidence is low: `atomically` (1385-1401) now aborts a torn `saveSnapshot`, `orphanSnapshotKeys()` collects such rows in `collectStale`, and `remove()` is only ever called by the SDK for a key whose `clientKey` segment embeds the current user. The neighbouring comment at 843-846 explicitly acknowledges "a header without one is a shape a torn write can produce", so the code already assumes the state is reachable.

verdict.reason: Line 838 does read `userId: header?.userId ?? this.userId`, but the cross-account harm is unreachable because the key space is per-account and the store's identity is the same identity embedded in that key. `remove()` has no app caller other than the SDK (grep over packages/ finds only the latch calls at durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:310/325 and test/contract helpers), and the SDK removes by its own `apiKey/clientKey/docKey`; that clientKey is `wb:{deviceSecret}:{userId}:{docKey}` (durable-session.ts:106-108), so another account's rows are under a different key and are never passed to remove(). The store's `this.userId` and the clientKey's userId both derive from the same `person.id`: collab-document-provider.tsx:228 feeds useDurableDocument, which builds the key synchronously from that prop (use-durable-document.ts:249), and the provider is mounted with the same id (collab-document-provider.tsx:366-367) while the store is memoized on it (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:148-189) — no lag window. Snapshots and headers are always written/deleted in one transaction (saveSnapshot 623-634 writing header.userId = this.userId at 629; purge 867-871; remove 847-849), so a headerless snapshot can only be a torn write at the removing client's own key, whose owner is this.userId. Hence the fallback restores the true owner rather than asserting a false one; listArchives (1066) / loadArchive (1090) / recoverOfflineCopy (offline-copy-recovery.ts:263-307) cannot surface another account's content. Genuinely foreign orphan rows are handled by the separate all-account sweep, which purges rather than archives (belongsToAnotherUser 1315-1317 -> orphanSnapshotKeys 1286-1297 -> collectStale 1238-1241). Skipping the archive when the header is absent remains harmless hardening, but it is not an exploitable authorization defect under this lens.

finding.summary: Offline-copy recovery silently falls back to `fetchWorkspaces()[0]`, which can publish a document's content into a shared team workspace the user does not own
finding.evidence:
`destinationWorkspace(undefined)` (offline-copy-recovery.ts:174-184) resolves to `(await fetchWorkspaces())[0]?.id` whenever the caller has no `workspaceId`. That branch is reached from `offline-runtime.tsx:271` whenever `fetchDocument(described.id)` answers 404 — i.e. the source document was deleted upstream, which the design names as one of the three ways an archive comes to exist at all.

The archive is a full snapshot of a CRDT document that lived in workspace A. `GET /workspaces` is `workspaceService.findAllByUser(userId)` (see packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.controller.ts:91 for the same call), which returns *every* workspace the user is a member of — including shared team workspaces, in whatever order the query yields. So the recovered copy, carrying workspace A's document content verbatim, is created in an arbitrary workspace B via `createWorkspaceDocument` (offline-copy-recovery.ts:225,242), where every other member of B can then read it.

Attacker/impact chain: no attacker is needed — a user clicks "Save a copy" on the toast (offline-runtime.tsx:285), the toast says only `Recovered as "<title>"` (offline-runtime.tsx:304) and never names the destination, and confidential content from a deleted private workspace lands in a workspace shared with colleagues. The user is given no opportunity to choose or even observe the destination before the write.

The design (docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md) justifies the fallback as "handing the work back somewhere beats refusing", but does not address that "somewhere" may be a multi-member workspace. Refusing, or prompting for a destination, would be the safe direction.

verdict.reason: The code is not as described. (1) The claimed silent fallback does not exist: `resolveRecoveryDestination` (offline-copy-recovery.ts:204-239) first enumerates workspaces and prefers one where the user is the sole member (`:225-236`, returning `shared:false`), and only then falls back to `workspaces[0]` (`:238`) — where it returns the workspace `name` and `shared: true`. It fails closed to `shared:true` when `fetchMe`/`fetchWorkspace` error (`:218-223`, `:227-228`) and throws when there is no workspace at all (`:211-213`). The literal `fetchWorkspaces()[0]` appears only at `:191` inside a comment describing the previous behavior. The cited lines 174-184 are the `RecoveryDestination` interface and a doc comment, not resolution logic. (2) The claim that the destination is never shown is false: offline-runtime.tsx:312-322 resolves the destination BEFORE rendering the offer, and :327-329 renders `Saving a copy puts them in "${destination.name}", which you share with other people.` whenever `destination.shared`. The click passes `workspaceId: destination.id` (:336), so the exact workspace named in the toast is the one written to and `destinationWorkspace` never re-resolves. (3) Enumerated all call sites: `destinationWorkspace` is called only at offline-copy-recovery.ts:285 and :302 from `recoverOfflineCopy`, whose only non-test caller is offline-runtime.tsx:333, which always supplies the resolved, disclosed id — no path reaches the bare fallback unguarded. (4) The design doc claim is also false: docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md:627-637 explicitly addresses the multi-member case and prescribes exactly the implemented sole-member preference plus named-destination disclosure, and tests offline-copy-recovery.test.ts:334-376 lock all three arms. The residual behavior (a copy can still reach a shared workspace when the user has no solo workspace) occurs only after the workspace is named to the user and they click to consent, which is disclosure-with-consent rather than the silent cross-tenant publication alleged.

finding.summary: The share-link PDF route mounts CollabDocumentProvider outside NonDurableScope, so the positional share-link durability gate does not cover it
finding.evidence: `SharedDocumentInner` returns `<SharedPdfLayout .../>` at shared-document.tsx:969 — an EARLY RETURN that happens before the `<NonDurableScope>` wrapper added at line 1017. `SharedPdfLayout` (line 753) mounts its own `YorkieProvider` and then `PdfCollabProvider`, which renders `CollabDocumentProvider` (app/files/pdf-collab.tsx:200). `useDurabilityPermitted()` therefore answers its default `true` (use-durable-document.ts:61) on that subtree. Today the route is saved only by the unrelated `isExcluded(docKey)` rule (`docKey.startsWith('pdf-')`, use-durable-document.ts:40-42), which the design states is temporary: docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md says PDF is "excluded until it has a chip". The moment that exclusion is lifted, a signed-in visitor on somebody else's share link gets the durable branch on this route — their own `wb:{salt}:{userId}:pdf-<id>` client authenticating with `fetchYorkieToken` (their personal token) rather than the share token whose role and expiry the auth webhook validates, and the shared document's comment content written to a disk the link's revocation cannot reach. That is precisely the bypass `NonDurableScope` was added to close, and the gate reads as covering the whole share route when it does not. `shared-document-durability.test.tsx` only exercises `resolved.type: 'sheet'`, so no test covers the pdf branch.

verdict.reason: The finding claims the pdf share-link route escapes the NonDurableScope because the scope sits inside SharedDocumentInner after the pdf early return. In this tree the scope is mounted in the CALLER: shared-document.tsx:1181-1183 wraps the entire <SharedDocumentInner/> in <NonDurableScope>, so the pdf early return at 968-981 (rendering SharedPdfLayout, defined at 743) is strictly below the provider and useDurabilityPermitted() resolves to false there. Line 1017, cited by the reviewer as the wrapper location, is actually the YorkieProvider's authTokenInjector prop; the in-code comments at 1008-1011 and 1174-1180 explicitly state the scope was moved above the branching precisely so the pdf return cannot step around it. A grep for SharedDocumentInner over all ts/tsx finds exactly one JSX mount (1182), and every other entry point (SharedDocument:1192, template-landing.tsx:174, template-review-queue.tsx:136) routes through SharedDocumentByToken, so there is no unguarded path to SharedPdfLayout. The claim that no test covers the pdf branch is also false: shared-document-durability.test.tsx:90-103 sets sharedType='pdf' and asserts permitted === false, with a default-is-true control at 105-112. The alleged bypass (durable branch with a personal fetchYorkieToken client on someone else's share link) therefore cannot occur even if the isExcluded('pdf-') rule at use-durable-document.ts:40-42 is lifted.
